nodes.title: Note:
widgets_values:
My recommendation is to convert all sRGB inputs to Rec.709 before sending them into the LTX 2.5 model. This helps preserve detail near black instead of producing unclamped black patches.

You have two options:

1. Use the OCIO Color Space node, as shown here.
2. In the OCIO Read node, keep the input color space set to sRGB and change the output color space to Rec.709.

nodes.title: Note:
widgets_values:
Use the custom **OCIO VAE Decode** node directly after the LTX 2.5 model.

This node was designed specifically to produce unclamped, clean Float32 output. It preserves values above 1.0 and, just as importantly, negative values below 0. These values are necessary for professional, scene-referred color workflows used in the film industry.

The node does not output sRGB. It outputs the same color space that was supplied to LTX 2.5, in this case Rec.709.

For this reason, set **From Color Space** to **Rec.709**, not sRGB. Otherwise, the image will appear darker.

This preserves the same color and tone as the input, but now in full range, with more available stops and higher lighting precision.

nodes.title: Note:
widgets_values:
There is one small tradeoff with this method.

If you want harder, brighter highlights, do not convert the input to Rec.709 before LTX 2.5. Send it into the model as **sRGB**.

Then, in the already connected **OCIO Write** node, set `From_ColorSpace` to **sRGB** instead of Rec.709.

The tradeoff is that some detail in the darker areas will be lost.

Lifehack:
When working in sRGB, try lifting the black point slightly above zero. This gives LTX 2.5 information in the darkest areas, so it can generate detail there instead of treating them as empty black patches.

nodes.title: OCIO VAE Decode - unclamped, replaces VAEDecodeTiled
OCIO LogConvert - LogC3 to linear, replaces their HDR node
Note: what stage 2 does
widgets_values:
## Stage 2 - LTX-2.3 HDR IC-LoRA

Stage 1 above generates with **LTX-2.5**. This stage converts those frames to linear HDR with **LTX-2.3 + `ic-lora-hdr-0.9`**, which is the only HDR path Lightricks ship for ComfyUI - there is no HDR workflow or LoRA for 2.5 in their pack as of their 2026-08-11 update.

**How it works.** The IC-LoRA takes ordinary SDR frames as a video guide and emits **ARRI LogC3**; their `LTXV HDR Decode Postprocess` undoes that curve and hands out linear. Nothing is log-encoded on the way in - their `LogC3.compress` is never called in the ComfyUI path.

**Why OCIO Write instead of their `save_exr`.** Their node writes with `cv2.imwrite` on BGR-flipped data and no colour transform. OCIO Write reads the frames as `Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)`, converts to `ACEScg` and lands **EXR 32f** with a metadata sidecar. That mapping is what the `LTX 2.3 HDR` profile does; it is set by hand here only because the profile also forces 16f, and this graph is meant for measuring.

**Cost.** Two 22B models in one graph. ComfyUI unloads stage 1 before stage 2, but expect a long run and drop the resolution first if VRAM is tight.

nodes.title: Note: level and primaries vs the LTX-2.5 graph
widgets_values:
## Reading these EXRs next to the LTX-2.5 ones

The scene-linear write in this graph uses `view = (none) colorimetric, no tone map`: the values are
carried by a colour transform and nothing else. The LTX-2.5 graph's EXR write
(`OCIO_WORKFLOW_LTX_2.5.json`, the `$OUTPUT/EXR_SEQ` node) instead uses
`view = ACES 1.3: ACES 1.0 - SDR Video`, which **inverts** the ACES output transform to get back to
scene-linear.

Both are legitimate and both are called scene-linear, but they are calibrated differently, so the two
sequences will not sit at the same level. Measured on one run, same scene, 25 frames:

| quantile | ACES-inverted write | colorimetric write | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| p1 | 0.00542 | 0.00161 | 3.36 |
| p50 | 0.08341 | 0.03348 | 2.49 |
| p90 | 0.34212 | 0.24907 | 1.37 |
| p99 | 2.96199 | 3.67842 | 0.81 |

The ratio is not constant - 3.4x in the shadows, 0.8x at p99 - so **no single exposure offset makes
them match**. It is a different curve, not a different level. Expect roughly 1.3-1.5 stops darker at
mid grey here, and grade accordingly rather than treating it as a fault.

Which one to prefer: this one is the physical answer, because the curve was undone by the transform
that encoded it. The ACES-inverted one is the practical answer for SDR generations, where no encoded
curve exists to undo. Pick per shot, and keep one choice across a sequence.

**Primaries matter as much as the curve.** `OCIO LogConvert` undoes a transfer curve only; it never
moves primaries. Whatever went in comes out in the same primaries, which on these paths is Rec.709 -
so the write's `input_colorspace` must say `Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)`, not `ACEScg`. Getting that wrong
makes the write a no-op and leaves Rec.709 numbers in a file labelled ACEScg: measured at +20% chroma
and red high by 10.5%, with luminance almost unchanged, which is exactly the kind of error that looks
like a grade rather than a bug.

nodes.title: Note: sRGB for text-to-video, Rec.709 for image-to-video
widgets_values:
## Set the display colorspace by what you fed the model

This graph ships wired for **image-to-video**, where `OCIO Color Space` converts the input plate
`sRGB - Display` -> `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` before the model. Because the input was converted,
the output is read back the same way: every node downstream that treats the decode as a display
signal is set to `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display`.

**Switch to text-to-video and that stops being true.** There is no input plate, so no conversion
happens, and the model emits its own native, sRGB-like signal. Every display colorspace on the
output side must then say `sRGB - Display`:

| node | image-to-video | text-to-video |
|---|---|---|
| `OCIO Write` (ProRes) in/out | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| `OCIO Write` (EXR) input | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| `OCIO Player` in/out | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |
| any `OCIO Color Space` reading the decode | `Rec.1886 Rec.709 - Display` | `sRGB - Display` |

Linear colorspaces are unaffected: `Linear Rec.709 (sRGB)` already names both, because Rec.709 and
sRGB share primaries and differ only in transfer.

**What it costs to get wrong.** Measured on a text-to-video run read as Rec.1886 instead of sRGB, the
sequence needed x8.52 to reach mid grey where the reference needed x2.97 - about 1.5 stops adrift, and
it looks like a grading problem rather than a settings one. Read correctly as sRGB the same pair came
out at x1.21 and x0.96, which is a match.

`bypass` on `LTXV Img To Video Inplace` is what makes the graph text-to-video: their code does
`if bypass: return (latent,)` (`comfy_extras/nodes_lt.py`), so the input image and every colour
conversion in front of it are skipped entirely.

nodes.title: Note: why the stock decode and their HDR node are not used
widgets_values:
## Why this stage does not use their two nodes

The obvious way to build this stage is `VAEDecodeTiled` -> `LTXV HDR Decode Postprocess`, which is
what their own example does. Both nodes clamp, and on log-encoded material that is expensive.

**Clamp 1, in ComfyUI itself.** `comfy/sd.py` builds every VAE with
`process_output = lambda image: image.add_(1.0).div_(2.0).clamp_(0.0, 1.0)`. Measured on this graph,
the decoder hands out values up to **1.16**, and the stock path cuts every one of them at 1.0.

**Clamp 2, in their node.** `hdr.py` does `logc = torch.clamp((z + 1.0) / 2.0, 0.0, 1.0)` before the
LogC3 decode. It never fires in practice, because clamp 1 already removed everything it would catch.

**Why a tiny overshoot matters here.** LogC3 is exponential near code 1.0: the curve's ceiling at
code 1.0 is 55.08, while code 1.16 decodes past 240. So 0.08% of samples, worth about a twentieth of
a stop on display-referred material, is worth **1.84 stops** once the log curve is undone. The pack's
own `OCIO VAE Decode` docstring is right that the node does not rescue range on ordinary material -
this is the case where it does.

**The replacements, both already in this pack:**

| stock node | replaced by | why |
|---|---|---|
| `VAEDecodeTiled` | `OCIO VAE Decode`, `clamp = False`, float32 | keeps values above 1.0 and below 0 |
| `LTXV HDR Decode Postprocess` | `OCIO LogConvert`, `Log to Linear`, `ARRI LogC3` | same published constants, no clamp on either end |

**Measured, one frame at 1280x704, brightest 0.1% of frame:**

| | stock chain | this chain |
|---|---|---|
| distinct values | 46 | **334** |
| range there | 0.03 stops | **0.82 stops** |
| pixels at the maximum | 259 (a plateau) | **1** (a real peak) |

**What this does not fix, stated plainly:** the disc keeps a wide shoulder of nearly constant value.
A horizontal profile across it sits between code 0.995 and 1.002 - about 54 linear - over roughly half
its width, so the model's gradation there is shallow and this chain cannot deepen it.

**What it does fix, which an earlier version of this note got wrong:** the shoulder is not the whole
disc. In the unclamped chain the core reaches code 1.1168, which is 163.5 linear, 1.57 stops above the
shoulder; pixels above code 1.01 make up 1.086% of a 121x121 box on the disc against 0.005% of the rest
of the frame. The stock chain reports the disc as uniformly flat only because it removed that core.

nodes.title: Render size and how to view the EXRs
widgets_values:
## Render size: set it on ResolutionSelector, not on Width / Height

Width and Height are PrimitiveInt nodes whose `value` input is **wired from
ResolutionSelector**, so typing a number into them does nothing. Change `megapixels` on
the selector instead.

**There is a trap in that dial.** Both stages halve the size (`a/2`) into the base latent
and a x2 latent upsampler brings it back, so **width and height must each be divisible by
64**, not 32. Values that look fine and are not:

| megapixels | 16:9, multiple 32 | halves | usable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.23 | 640 x 384 | 320 / 192 | yes |
| 0.24 | 672 x 384 | 336 / 192 | **no**, 336 is not a multiple of 32 |
| 0.25 | 672 x 384 | 336 / 192 | **no** |
| **0.26** | **704 x 384** | 352 / 192 | **yes, this run** |
| 0.90 | 1280 x 720 | 640 / 360 | **no**, 360 is not a multiple of 32 |

Computed from `comfy_extras/nodes_resolution.py`, which rounds
`sqrt(megapixels * 1024 * 1024 / (w * h)) * ratio` to the nearest multiple.

## Viewing the result

The two EXR sequences are **scene-linear ACEScg**. Do not open them expecting a picture:
clipping them to 0..1 for display throws away the whole range the HDR stage produced, and
a clipped HDR frame looks identical to the SDR frame it came from. View through an ACES
output transform, and change exposure in **linear**, before that transform, never after.


## Stage-1 decode: temporal_size 64, not 4096

`temporal_size` is in **frames**, and the VAE has an 8x temporal ratio, so the tile is
`temporal_size / 8` **latent** frames. The value this workflow used to ship, 4096, means
512 latent frames, i.e. **no temporal tiling at all**: the whole clip decodes in one chunk.

Measured at 704 x 384 on a 24 GB card:

| frames | temporal_size | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 49 | 4096 | 5.5 min |
| 73 | 4096 | 5.8 min |
| 121 | 4096 | **wedges**: card pinned at 23.6 of 24 GB, no log line for an hour, server stops answering |
| 121 | **64** | **6.8 min** |

The seam risk that 4096 was avoiding does not come back at 64. Frame-to-frame difference
was checked at periods of 8, 16 and 64 frames across all 121 frames of both sequences: the
largest ratio against the surrounding frames was 1.10x, well under the 1.8x a real seam
produces.

nodes.title: Published values restored
widgets_values:
## Published values restored

This file carries the author's numbers, not the ones a 24 GB card needed while this was
being worked out. What was reverted, and what it was reverted from:

| node | widget | local | published |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 403 ResolutionSelector | megapixels | 0.26 (704x384) | **0.9** (1280x720) |
| 455 OCIO VAE Decode | temporal_size | 64 | **4096** |

Both published values assume the memory is there and the size divides cleanly. If the card
runs out, or if the resolution dial hands you a size the base latent rejects, the note
titled *Render size and how to view the EXRs* carries the measurements behind both numbers
and says what to change instead.

nodes.title: Levels: the HDR pass sits lower
widgets_values:
## The HDR pass sits BELOW the SDR master, and by how much depends on the shot

Put the two side by side at the same exposure and the HDR looks like a different gamma. It
is not a gamma and it is not a fault. The pass does not correct the plate, it re-renders it
into a different tonal distribution: shadows and mid-tones come down, highlights go up.

Measured on six shots, taking median luminance at five frames spread through each clip:

| shot | SDR median | HDR median | lift |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cyberpunk portrait, neon | 0.0647 | 0.0219 | **1.56 stops** |
| the same shot, camera panned onto the city | 0.0688 | 0.0230 | **1.58 stops** |
| dragon in a cave, fire from the mouth | 0.0665 | 0.0291 | **1.23 stops** |
| city street, traffic, sun down the street | 0.0896 | 0.0449 | **0.98 stops** |
| cave mouth, a figure, a ship beyond | 0.1254 | 0.0645 | **0.97 stops** |
| glass towers, sun in the gap | 0.1697 | 0.1157 | **0.55 stops** |

**Over a full stop separates them**, 0.55 to 1.58, so a number baked from one shot is wrong
on the next.

**Whether one number holds for a whole shot depends on the camera.** Where the framing is
held it is steady: across the clip the portrait varied 3.0% and the dragon 4.8%. Where the
camera travels onto a different subject it is not: the pan off the figure onto the city
varied 45.3%, and the dolly-and-tilt up the street 30.2%. On a moving shot, measure at
several frames and then either animate the value or accept the drift knowingly.

## Measure it, do not assume it

Median luminance of the SDR divided by median luminance of the HDR is the lift. Apply it
downstream - a Grade or a Multiply in Nuke - not in this graph. Nothing here should bake a
viewing decision into a scene-linear master.

## What the lift reveals

On the portrait, after matching mid-tones:

| percentile | SDR | HDR lifted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 25 | 0.036 | 0.028 (deeper) |
| 50 | 0.066 | 0.066 (matched) |
| 90 | 0.219 | **0.448** |
| 99 | 1.507 | **4.482** |

Area above 1.0 linear goes from 2.44% to 5.83%. The peak is clean too: 14.0, where the raw
plate reached 32,240 on a handful of pixels that are decoder noise rather than light. So the
headroom is real. It simply sits lower, and wants one number per shot to line up.

nodes.title: OCIO Exposure - match the HDR to the plate (0 = untouched)
Exposure: what to put in it
widgets_values:
## Exposure: neutral on purpose

`exposure` is in **stops** and this node ships at **0.0**, which is a pass-through. It
contains no clamp at all. That is not a reading of the widget name, it is what the pack's
own `nodes.py` does:

```python
out[..., :3] = arr[..., :3] * gain      # gain = 2.0 ** exposure, and that is all
```

No clamp appears anywhere in the node, and `tools/test_exposure.py` holds it to that: a
value of 12.0 at +1 stop must come out 24.0 and a negative must stay negative, with a
control showing a clamped result would fail both.

## What to put in it, and how to find that number

The HDR pass sits BELOW the SDR master, by an amount that depends on the shot. Measured on
six shots it ran from **0.55** to **1.58** stops.

Find it as the ratio of median luminance, SDR over HDR, then take log2. Two warnings come
with that number. Do not carry it over from another shot, because over a stop separates the
six. And do not assume it holds for a whole shot: it does where the framing is held, varying
3.0% and 4.8% on two such clips, and it does not where the camera travels onto a different
subject, varying 45.3% on a pan and 30.2% on a dolly and tilt.

## Leave it at zero unless you mean it

At 0.0 the master stays exactly what the decode produced, and the lift belongs in the grade
where it can still be changed. Set it here only when the deliverable is meant to sit at the
plate's level and nobody downstream will be matching it.

nodes.title: Generate, then convert: read this first
widgets_values:
# One graph, two halves: generate, then convert

The left two thirds are the repository's own `OCIO_WORKFLOW_LTX_2.5.json`, unchanged. It
generates from the start frame and writes the SDR deliverables:

| node | what it writes |
| --- | --- |
| 461 OCIO Write | ProRes 4444, Rec.1886, no tone map - the review |
| 471 OCIO Write | EXR sequence, 32f, ACEScg - the scene-linear master |

**Those writers stay.** The SDR pair is a deliverable in its own right, not scaffolding.

The same decode that feeds them also feeds the HDR half on the right, so the second stage
runs on the frames already in memory.

## Where the guide comes from, and why not from the EXR

The IC-LoRA guide is taken from node 455, the decode, which is display-referred and peaks
near 1.08. That is what an SDR guide is.

The EXR written beside it is **not** interchangeable with it. Node 471 writes Rec.1886 to
ACEScg, which crosses display to scene, so the ACES view runs INVERSE and expands the range:
the file peaks in the hundreds. Feeding that back as a guide was tried and the run completed
without an error, producing a sequence peaking near **200 million**. The LogC3 decode tops out
near 55 at code 1.0; a guide fifteen times too hot is far outside its domain.

If you split this graph in two and drive the HDR half from files, read the **ProRes**, not
the EXR sequence, and make sure the movie carries every frame: LTX needs a length of the
form 8k+1, so a 48-frame guide rounds DOWN to 41 and the second half silently returns a
shorter clip.

## Two things to read before you run it

**Memory.** Both models are resident at once here, and that is the one way this graph bites
on a smaller card. The note titled *Render size and how to view the EXRs* carries the
measurements and the single setting to change.

**Levels.** The HDR half comes back below the plate and needs its own number, measured on
this shot rather than carried over. `OCIO Exposure` sits before the HDR writers at 0.0, a
pass-through. The note titled *Levels: the HDR pass sits lower* has the measurements, and
the reason a shot with a big camera move needs more care than one number.
